name: Project Management Professional (PMP)®
title: PMP Exam Preparation
lead: Everything you need to prepare for the PMP exam in one place: what the exam covers, a study approach that works, five free full-length simulators with 900 original questions, and the guides to go with them.
heroAlt: Candidate taking a computer-based exam with project charts floating around the workstation

facts.text: domains: People, Process and Business Environment
free practice questions in five full PMPORT mocks

outline.name: People
outline.items: Leading teams, managing conflict, engaging and aligning stakeholders, communication and knowledge transfer.

outline.name: Process
outline.items: Planning and integration, scope, value delivery, resources, procurement, finance, quality, schedule, status and closure.

outline.name: Business Environment
outline.items: Governance, compliance, change control, impediments, risk, continuous improvement, organizational change and external changes.

audience: Project managers who lead and direct projects and want the most widely recognized project management certification.
eligibility: PMI requires project leadership experience (typically 36 months with a four-year degree, or 60 months with a secondary diploma) and 35 contact hours of project management education. Always check PMI's current PMP handbook before applying.
format: Scenario-based questions across predictive, agile and hybrid approaches
Multiple choice, multiple response, matching, hotspot and graphic-based items
Case studies that test how you apply judgement in context

plan.title: Weeks 1–2: Learn the outline
plan.text: Read the exam content outline and the PMBOK® Guide principles. Take one simulator in practice mode to find your weak domains.

plan.title: Weeks 3–4: Build the mindset
plan.text: Study the PMP mindset: servant leadership, value, collaboration and tailoring. Drill the People domain by task.

plan.title: Weeks 5–6: Process and agile
plan.text: Work through planning, schedule, cost, risk and agile practices. Practise the project maths with the calculators.

plan.title: Weeks 7–8: Full mocks
plan.text: Take full timed mocks, review every wrong answer and aim for a consistent 75% or more before booking the exam.

related.label: Free PMP study guide and 8-week plan

faq.q: How hard is the PMP exam?
faq.a: It is demanding because questions test judgement in realistic situations, not memorization. Regular full-length practice is the best preparation.

faq.q: Are the PMPORT questions real exam questions?
faq.a: No. They are original practice questions written to the public exam content outline. Real exam questions are confidential.

outline.name: Project Management Fundamentals and Core Concepts
outline.items: Life cycles and processes, planning, roles and responsibilities, following planned strategies, and problem-solving tools.

outline.items: When to use a predictive approach, the project schedule, and documenting project controls.

outline.name: Agile Frameworks/Methodologies

plan.title: Week 2: Predictive planning

plan.title: Week 3: Agile

faq.q: Should I take the CAPM or the PMP?
faq.a: The CAPM suits people early in their career with little project experience. The PMP requires several years of project leadership experience.

faq.q: Does the CAPM include business analysis?
faq.a: Yes. Business analysis frameworks are 27% of the exam, so study requirements, stakeholders and roadmaps as well as project management.

name: PMI Risk Management Professional (PMI-RMP)®
title: Risk Management (PMI-RMP) Exam Preparation
lead: Get ready for the PMI-RMP® exam. Learn what each of the five risk domains covers, follow a six-week study plan, revise the key risk formulas and practise with three free full-length simulators: 345 original questions weighted like the real exam.
heroAlt: A probability and impact heat map with risk markers, a risk trend line and an S-curve on a project risk dashboard

facts.text: domains, from risk planning to closing risks
free practice questions in three full PMPORT mocks

outline.name: Risk Identification
outline.items: Identification workshops, prompt lists such as PESTLE, checklists, SWOT, Delphi and premortems; assumption and constraint analysis; specific, measurable triggers; cause-event-effect risk statements; and building a useful risk register with one accountable owner per risk.

outline.name: Risk Analysis
outline.items: Qualitative analysis with probability and impact scales and the P-I matrix; other parameters such as urgency, manageability, detectability and connectivity; data quality and bias; quantitative analysis with EMV, three-point (PERT) estimates, decision trees, Monte Carlo simulation, S-curves and tornado charts; threats, opportunities, variability, ambiguity and overall project risk.

outline.name: Risk Strategy and Planning
outline.items: Reviewing the charter, business case, contracts and lessons learned; assessing the internal and external environment; turning risk appetite into measurable thresholds; tailoring the risk process to the project; writing the risk management plan; and leading risk work with stakeholders.

outline.name: Monitor and Close Risks
outline.items: Using performance data (earned value, trends, technical measures, agile metrics) to spot risks; reserve analysis; monitoring residual and secondary risks and the watch list; risk audits and reviews; updating the register and risk report; tracking overall risk against thresholds; closing risks and capturing lessons learned.

outline.name: Risk Response
outline.items: Threat strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, escalate, accept) and opportunity strategies (exploit, enhance, share, escalate, accept); contingency and fallback plans; cost-effective, owned responses; funding from contingency reserve; and checking that implemented responses work.

audience: Project managers, risk analysts and specialists who lead or support risk management on projects and programs and want to show specialist risk skills.
eligibility: PMI asks for project risk experience plus risk management education: typically 36 months of risk experience and 40 contact hours with a secondary degree, or 24 months and 30 contact hours with a four-year degree, within the last five years. Check PMI's current PMI-RMP handbook before applying.
format: 15 of the questions are unscored pretest items
Scenario questions plus EMV, PERT, decision tree and Monte Carlo interpretation

plan.title: Week 1: Strategy and planning
plan.text: Learn risk appetite versus thresholds, tailoring, the contents of a risk management plan and the roles of sponsor, risk owner and action owner.

plan.title: Week 2: Identification
plan.text: Practise writing cause-event-effect risk statements, run through prompt lists (PESTLE, TECOP), assumption analysis and triggers, and design a risk register.

plan.title: Week 3: Qualitative analysis
plan.text: Master probability and impact scales, the P-I matrix, urgency, manageability and connectivity, and how bias distorts ratings.

plan.title: Week 4: Quantitative analysis
plan.text: Work through EMV, PERT mean and standard deviation, decision trees, P50/P80 on S-curves, tornado charts and contingency from confidence levels.

plan.title: Week 5: Responses, monitoring and closing
plan.text: Learn each threat and opportunity strategy, contingency and fallback plans, secondary and residual risk, reserve analysis, audits and risk reports.

plan.title: Week 6: Full mocks
plan.text: Take all three timed mocks, review every explanation and drill weak domains in practice mode until you score 75% or more consistently.

faq.q: Which formulas do I need for the PMI-RMP exam?
faq.a: Expected monetary value (probability × impact, negative for threats and positive for opportunities), PERT mean (O + 4M + P) / 6, triangular mean (O + M + P) / 3, PERT standard deviation (P − O) / 6, variance (standard deviation squared) and decision tree expected values. You should also be able to read P50 and P80 values from an S-curve.

faq.q: What is the difference between a risk threshold and a trigger?
faq.a: A threshold is the limit of acceptable risk for an objective, agreed with stakeholders in the risk management plan. A trigger is a warning sign that one specific risk is about to happen, recorded in the register so the owner knows when to act.

faq.q: How is the PMI-RMP different from the PMP?
faq.a: The PMP covers all of project management. The PMI-RMP goes deep into one area: planning, identifying, analyzing, responding to and monitoring project risk, including quantitative techniques.
